title: Cheaper AI tokens are driving more demand, and that's Jensen Huang's best-case scenario
source_used: The Decoder (full text from the main session's fulltext copy; a short article)
key_facts: Data from Ornn, Silicon Data and Bloomberg (as of August 2026) shows what the venture firm a16z calls a textbook Jevons paradox in the AI market.
Token prices keep dropping, but rental prices for H100 GPUs (Nvidia AI chips) hold steady or climb.
Cheaper tokens unlock AI agents, automation and new applications, so volume grows faster than per-unit costs fall.
It is not clear how much demand comes from humans and how much from AI systems themselves, since agentic AI uses tokens at a very high rate.
The whole picture rests on AI usage growing fast enough to offset falling token prices; if demand flattens, chip makers, memory suppliers, energy providers and cloud companies take a hit.
The Decoder says markets are already sensitive: US stocks dropped on reports that OpenAI's annualized revenue might be lower than previously reported.
quote_evidence: Token prices keep dropping, but H100 GPU rental prices hold steady or climb.
The whole system rests on one assumption: AI usage has to grow fast enough to offset falling token prices.
How much demand comes from humans versus the systems themselves isn't clear, since agentic AI burns through tokens at a staggering rate.
why_it_matters_hint: Cheaper AI is raising demand for AI computing rather than lowering it, which keeps chips scarce and expensive as long as use keeps growing.
event_date: Data as of August 2026; The Decoder published 11 Oct 2026; the date of a16z's analysis is not stated
notes: Short article (about 1,300 characters), read in full. a16z's own analysis was not read; the Decoder is the only outlet. Background not in the article: a16z is Andreessen Horowitz, H100 is Nvidia's AI chip, and Jensen Huang is Nvidia's chief executive. The OpenAI revenue reports mentioned are covered in today's edition (see C07-01).
